---
title: "Data-driven archetypes of farmland change: Preliminary results"
author: Carolyn Koehn
abstract: |
  Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of global land was converted from agriculture to highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018. The processes leading to this conversion are variable, but most farmland protection policy focuses on controlling urban sprawl. A better understanding of the multiple contexts in which farmland loss occurs can inform the development of more diverse policies for agricultural land protection. We used an interdisciplinary archetypes approach that identifies recurring patterns of variables in social-ecological systems across different spaces and time periods. We combined finite Gaussian mixture model cluster analysis and qualitative case studies to find recurring patterns of change over time in 26 counties in southern Idaho's Snake River Plain, a region of the western United States [US] with both high agricultural production and high population growth where agricultural lands are at risk of conversion. We chose data linked to second-tier variables in the resource and actors subsystems in Ostrom’s social-ecological systems framework. Specifically, we calculated descriptive metrics for 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 from the US Census, land use/land cover spatial data, and the US Census of Agriculture. We found that these 26 counties over 4 time points clustered into 6 resource clusters and 3 actors clusters. Resource clusters were strongly driven by developed land, housing density, and jobs supporting agriculture, whereas actor clusters were strongly driven by residents with a Bachelor’s degree, workers in manufacturing, and average age. We then selected 4 counties from the full pool of counties to do qualitative case study analysis and link those insights with the results of the data driven clusters. Through combined quantitative and qualitative approaches, we found that agricultural land loss occurs in multiple contexts, including urban sprawl and in more rural areas with recreation access. We reveal spatially distant counties in the same archetype that may be able to share successful farmland protection policies, as well as neighboring counties in different archetypes that will likely require different policy pathways to protect farmland. We intentionally used publicly available data so that this approach could be applied to many areas grappling with agricultural land loss.
date: last-modified

# Introduction

Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of land has been converted from agriculture to urban and highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018, amounting to 7.5% of total global land cover change in that 25-year period [@radwan2021]. The pathway to conversion is often attributed to urban or suburban sprawl [@chen2020; @vanvliet2017], and land use projections are based on the assumption that population growth will drive urban development of agricultural lands based on their proximity to an urban center [@xie2023; @chen2020; @haney2015]. However, there are other pathways to agricultural land conversion, such as housing development in rural settlements and increased construction of commodity processing and transportation facilities, that are rarely addressed alongside urban sprawl in land use change literature (for exceptions, see @ju2018 and @jiang2019). Even when other pathways to agricultural land loss impact a smaller land area compared urban sprawl, they can have significant negative impacts on local ecology and crop production [@zhu2022] and social well-being [@smith2001]. In order to protect high quality agricultural lands, it is critical to understand the multiple pathways that those lands are converted to other uses. There are three recurring patterns of farmland loss that have been described separately in a number of case studies: urban/suburban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization.

Urban sprawl is a widely recognized pathway to agricultural land loss. As population in urban centers grow, there is increased need for housing. While cities may create denser housing in the urban center to accommodate a larger population, they often expand outwards onto marginal lands as affluent, car-owning residents seek spacious suburban neighborhoods [@dieleman2004]. As suburbs encroach on agricultural land, farmland fragmentation makes farming more difficult and encourage further development [@latruffe2014; @qiu2015; @freedgood2020]. As near-urban farmlands rise in value, the number of senior producers far exceeds the number of young producers, and as demographic and culture changes make farming less appealing, the sale of agricultural lands to urban developers is an attractive offer [@kuethe2014; @freedgood2020; @sheridan2007]. High quality croplands are especially susceptible to urban sprawl as both farming and housing development are easiest on flat lands with more access to freshwater [@halperin2023; @bren2017]. Urban and suburban sprawl are a prominent cause of agricultural lands loss and are present in many land use change models focused on agricultural lands [@xie2023; @chen2020; @haney2015].

Industrial expansion is seen as a vehicle for economic growth and it has manifested diversely in different global regions. Across Asia, conversion of agricultural land to industry use precedes urban sprawl or occurs alongside urban sprawl [@azadi2011; @tuyen2013; @zhou2020]. In Europe, a large portion of manufacturing was shifted to rural areas in the late 1970s [@keeble1983]. In the United States, supply-oriented food manufacturing (e.g. cheese manufacturing) is likely to occur in rural agricultural areas with sufficient infrastructure and labor availability [@lambert2009]. Additionally, manufacturing facilities tend to agglomerate around certain urban or local economies so that the presence of one manufacturing facility is correlated with the presence of more [@lambert2009]. Besides conversion of agricultural land for manufacturing facilities, these factories attract non-local workers who will need housing, yet their settlement patterns may be different from those of urban migrants. For example, rural industrial restructuring is linked with Hispanic growth [@lichter2012]. Thus, the industrial expansion pathway to agricultural land loss manifests in a different manner than agricultural conversion due to urban sprawl. 

Amenity migration, the migration of affluent urban populations to rural areas for specific lifestyle amenities, is a pathway to rural land change, including agricultural land loss [@abrams2012]. Rural sprawl associated with amenity migration is less dense than urban sprawl, resulting in larger areas of land affected, but with less intensity [@radeloff2005]. Amenity migrants with agricultural estates do not rely on agricultural production as a means of income, and may engage in some form of farming (including hobby farms), lease lands to local producers, or use their lands for non-production uses like recreation and conservation [@abrams2012; @abrams2013]. Local jobs are primarily low-wage service jobs, and this combined with rising property values can push low income households farther out of the high-amenity community [@sherman2018; @loeffler2007; @abrams2012]. Thus, agricultural producers in high amenity communities may face rising costs and falling off-farm wages, the need to lease land, and the fragmentation of agricultural lands by migrant estates and commuter roads. Amenity migration is a distinct pathway to agricultural land loss that differs in cause and effects from urban sprawl and industrial expansion, and requires different policy and planning approaches to address.

Since agricultural land conversion occurs via different processes in different contexts, farmland loss may be best described by archetype analysis. Archetypes are recurring patterns of social-ecological variables that build towards middle-range theories -- generalizations that describe causal pathways within a well-bounded range of phenomena [@meyfroidt2018; @oberlack2019]. The three farmland loss pathways described above, urban/suburban sprawl, agricultural industrialization, and amenity migration, will require context-specific policies to control farmland conversion, and places with similar patterns of farmland loss may share successful policies. However, to our knowledge, multiple archetypes of farmland loss have not been identified in a generalized yet spatially and temporally explicit manner across a single study region. In the United States, long-term public datasets enable longitudinal studies of land use and demographic change that can construct dynamic archetypes, patterns of social-ecological variables that re-occur across both space and time. The intentional use of public data ensures that this analysis can be implemented across the country.

The Snake River Plain of Idaho is an ideal place to study multiple processes of farmland loss because it is experiencing different drivers of agricultural land conversion across its counties. We hypothesize that land use change is occurring due to urban/suburban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization in different areas across the region. This research will aid in identifying where distinct processes of land use change are occurring, contributing to a diverse toolbox for agricultural lands protection in diverse localities. We calculated descriptive metrics for 26 Idaho counties in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 (104 units total) from the US Census, land use/land cover spatial data, and the US Census of Agriculture. Our research questions were:

1. Are there identifiable archetypes of social-ecological subsystems (resource and actors) in Idaho's Snake River Plain?
2. What are those archetypes, and which demographic, economic, and remotely sensed indicators are the most important characteristics of those archetypes?
3. What is the relationship between these archetypes and farmland loss?
4. Are there counties that have shifted archetypes through time, and what are their characteristics?

# Methods

## Data Selection

We linked data available from 1990-2020 to second-tier variables in Ostrom's social-ecological systems framework [@ostrom2009] based on expert knowledge from the authors. Some second-tier variables are excluded because no relevant data sources could be found. Detailed data processing steps and sources for all data tables for each indicator and year can be found in Appendix A.

I scaled these data by mean normalization (divided by the range), so that all variables had a mean of 0 and range of [-1, 1]. In clustering, dividing by the range (scaling) is preferable to dividing by the standard deviation (normalization) to preserve possible cluster structure in the data [@hennig2016].

## Clustering

### Algorithmic Variable Selection

Before clustering begins, it is useful to select the most important variables for clustering. The `clustvarsel` package uses methods to select the most optimal subset of variables that contain cluster information and suggest variables that provide little extra information to drop. It's important to note that these are locally optimal -- depending on where in parameter space the algorithm randomly starts, it is possible that different variables may be selected. To account for this, I ran the variable selection algorithm 20 times and used the list of variables most frequently selected between the 20 runs.

I chose the most conservative method. The algorithm starts with all the variables, and tests dropping different variables from the equation to see if the difference is minimal.

I tested for a range of 1-5 possible clusters. It's recommended to vary the number of possible clusters between 1 and the next integer after $n^{0.3}$ [4 < 104$^{0.3}$ < 5, @biernacki2006].

From the Resource clusters, the following variables were removed: lake area and jobs supporting agriculture.

From the Actors clusters, the following variables were removed: percent retired, average age, residents with a high school education, farm tenure status, and racial composition.

### Gaussian Model-Based Clustering

To select a model, which includes selecting the number of groups and the shape, I used BIC to test 14 different model shapes and 1-5 possible clusters.

Since this clustering finds local maxima, it is sensitive to its initialization. I ran the cluster models 200 times for each SES subsystem, preserving the best model as the final result.

3 clusters was the best fit for the resource data. 3 clusters was the best fit for the resource data.

The log likelihood values from the bootstrapping process indicate that there are no competing models, so the final models are very likely to be the global as well as local maxima.

# Preliminary Results

## Cluster Descriptions

Each cluster corresponds to an archetype. For an archetype analysis, not only do you assign each cluster a name, but you also tell a unifying narrative of the units in that cluster. I've done my best to describe the defining attributes of each cluster and tell a short unifying narrative about each one.

### Resource Clusters

#| label: "label county data"

#### Cluster R1: Urban sprawl and amenity migration counties have similar resource systems

<!-- check for accuracy with new model

Characteristic resources of R1 are a higher presence of forest, developed, and recreation land and proximity to recreation destinations like ski areas and national parks (@fig-R-CIs). These counties have experienced higher cropland loss and developed land gain compared to other resource clusters, though they have lost less farms, and sometimes even gained farms, compared to the rest of the study area (@fig-R-CIs, @supptblb-data-R1). In general, cluster R1 exhibits wide ranges in its data indicators, showing that counties in this cluster are similar but not homogeneous (@suppfigb-R-ranges, @supptblb-data-R1). --> 

#### Cluster R2: Counties with large areas of isolated land

Characteristic resources of R2 are low housing and farm density, high presence of shrubland and federal land, and less land with access to a major roadway (@fig-R-CIs). Access to natural recreation areas like lakes, rivers, and ski areas is fairly low (@suppfigb-R-ranges, @supptblb-data-R1). There is low cropland cover and larger farms are more common, indicating that agriculture in these counties is more focused on livestock grazing. Many R2 counties are large (@fig-resource-cluster-map), and data on the large areas of isolated lands can mask the presence and growth of developed areas (e.g. the city of Twin Falls in Twin Falls county).

To characterize Actors cluster A1, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Higher than average population density (mean: `r round(0.194*247.1053814672, 0)` persons per $km^2$, min: `r round(0.00801*247.1053814672, 0)` persons per $km^2$ [Blaine, 1990], max: `r round(0.735*247.1053814672, 0)` persons per $km^2$ [Ada, 2020])
- Higher population gain (mean: +28%, min: +0.9% [Bannock, 1990], max: +74% [Teton, 2000])
- Higher than average percentage of residents with at least a Bachelors degree (mean: 30%, min: 12% [Canyon, 1990], max: 48% [Teton, 2020])
- Higher than average amount of farms with a net loss (mean: 60%, min: 46% [Madison, 2020], max: 79% [Ada, 2020])
- Higher than average percentage of the population living in an urban area (mean: 58%, min: 0% [Teton, 2000-10], max: 95% [Ada, 2010])
- The average PCA results indicate that in A1 many people are employed in services. construction and finance/insurance/real estate are also more likely. People tend not to be employed in manufacturing and wholesale trade.

Cluster A1 consists of Ada, Blaine, and Canyon counties in 1990-2020, Bannock and Bonneville counties in 1990-2010, Teton and Madison counties in 2000-2020, and Elmore County in 2000. In these counties and years, the number of actors in the system is generally increasing quickly. Most of the population is living in urban areas (although there is a wide range), and many have graduated college. The farming actors are at a financial disadvantage, as on average 60% of their farms operate at a net loss in any given year.

#### Cluster A2: Manufacturing provides additional rural employment

```{r}
#| eval: false

a2 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "A2")

a2_means <- a2 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Actors cluster A2, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Lower unemployment rate (mean: 4.9%, min: 3.4% [Jefferson], max: 5.6% [Payette])
- Higher percentage of people with a Bachelors degree (mean: 25%, min: 20% [Payette], max: 32% [Bonneville])
- More farms with net losses (mean: 64%, min: 56% [Twin Falls], max: 75% [Bannock])
- Lower urban population (mean: 14%, min: 9% [Gem], max: 19% [Elmore])
- A higher value of industry employment PC2 translates to a high percentage of people employed in manufacturing, and to a lesser degree, in services and in transportation and public utilities.

Cluster A2 consists of 8 counties in 2020: Bannock, Bingham, Bonneville, Elmore, Gem, Jefferson, Payette, and Twin Falls. Many here are employed in manufacturing, or support manufacturing in the services and transportation sectors. With many farms operating at a net loss, manufacturing can offer off-farm employment. This is the only cluster where unemployment is lower than the study area average, which could be because of these manufacturing jobs. A majority of the actors in these counties are living in rural areas, few are unemployed, and many have college degrees.

#### Cluster A3: Slow growing population in urban areas

```{r}
#| eval: false

a3 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "A3")

a3_means <- a3 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

To characterize Actors cluster A3, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Lower population density (mean: `r round(0.0286*247.1053814672, 0)` persons per $km^2$, min: `r round(0.0007*247.1053814672, 1)` persons per $km^2$ [Clark, 2020], max: `r round(0.0869*247.1053814672, 0)` persons per $km^2$ [Payette, 2010])
- Lower population growth (mean: +8%, min: -20% [Clark, 2020], max: +37% [Jefferson, 2010])
- Less residents have a Bachelors degree (mean: 14%, min: 7% [Gem, 1990], max: 22% [Fremont, 2020])
- Less farms operate at a net loss (mean: 48%, min: 31% [Minidoka, 1990], max: 67% [Payette, 2000])
- Higher percent of population living in urban areas (mean: 42%, min: 0% [Teton, 1990], max: 100% [Power, 1990])
- A higher value of industry employment PC2 translates to a high percentage of people employed in manufacturing, and to a lesser degree, in services and in transportation and public utilities. This value is not as high as in A2, so manufacturing is not as large of an industry. Here, PC1 is lower than in A2, indicating that the services industry in A3 employs less people. The mean PC values for PCs 1 and 2 also indicate that A3 employs a slightly higher percentage of people in agriculture.

Cluster A3 consists of Cassia, Fremont, Gooding, Jerome, Minidoka, Power, and Washington counties for 1990-2020. For 1990-2010, but not 2020, Bingham, Gem, Jefferson, Payette, and Twin Falls counties are in this cluster (these all transition to A2 in 2020). Owyhee County is in A3 for 2000-2020. A few counties also briefly are in A3: Clark and Lincoln counties in 2020, Madison and Teton counties in 1990, and Elmore County in 1990 and 2010 (Elmore also transitions to A2 in 2020).

The defining characteristic of this archetype seems to be slow population growth, an sometimes population decline, and low population density, but do contain an urban area where some to most of the population live (compared to A4, where population growth is also slow but the population is much more rural). Farmers in this cluster may have more power than in other clusters, as this is the cluster with the lowest percentage of farms operating at a net loss.

To characterize Actors cluster A4, I report its significantly different variables and their mean values from the raw data:

- Low population density (mean: `r round(0.0027*247.1053814672, 0)` persons per $km^2$, min: `r round(0.000675*247.1053814672, 1)` persons per $km^2$ [Clark, 1990], max: `r round(0.00677*247.1053814672, 0)` persons per $km^2$ [Lincoln, 2010])
- Low population growth (mean: +6%, min: -13% [Butte, 1990], +36% [Camas, 2000])
- Lower percentage of residents with Bachelors degree (mean: 16%, min: 9% [Owyhee, 1990], max: 27% [Camas, 2020])
- Very low urban population (mean: 0.75%, min: 0% [most counties], max: 5.5% [Camas, 2020])
- A low value for employment industries PC2 indicates low employment in manufacturing, services, and wholesale trade. The averaged PCA results for A4 suggest higher employment in agriculture and construction.

Cluster A4 consists of Adams, Butte, and Camas counties in 1990-2020, as well as Clark and Lincoln counties in 1990-2010, and Owyhee County in 1990. The low population density and low to nonexistent urban population suggest that this archetype is very rural, and the population here grows more slowly. The US Census defines "urban" by population and housing density, so once these counties' population centers crosses the census threshold, they likely transitioned to A3.

## Pairing Resource and Actor Archetypes

Each county in each analysis year has both a Resource archetype and an Actors archetype. Here, I try to link the two and describe overarching patterns of which resource systems and actor types are associated with each other.

```{r}
#| label: fig-RA-assoc
#| fig-cap: "Actors clusters present in each Resource cluster."
#| eval: false

county_clusts <- left_join(st_drop_geometry(clust_dat[["Resource"]][,c("county", "year", "cluster")]),
                          st_drop_geometry(clust_dat[["Actors"]][,c("county", "year", "cluster")]),
                          by = c("county", "year"),
                         suffix = c(".R", ".A"))

barcodes <- bind_rows(clust_dat) %>%
  select(county, year, cluster) %>%
  group_by(county, geometry, year) %>%
  mutate(yearcode = paste0(cluster, collapse = "")) %>%
  select(-cluster) %>%
  unique() %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county, geometry),
              names_from = year,
              values_from = yearcode) %>%
  select(county, `1990`, `2000`, `2010`, `2020`, geometry) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(barcode = paste(c_across(`1990`:`2020`), collapse = "-"))

# table(c(barcodes$`1990`, barcodes$`2000`, barcodes$`2010`, barcodes$`2020`))

ggplot(county_clusts, aes(x=cluster.A)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(vars(cluster.R)) +
  labs(x = "Actors Cluster", y="Count") +
  theme_bw()
```

Cluster R1 (counties near famous recreation areas represent the study area average of farmland loss, developed land gain) is associated with cluster A1 (more urbanites), A2 (manufacturing provides additional rural employment), and A3 (slow growing population in urban areas). Cluster R1 contains many counties, with different types of actors, yet they retain their resource similarities. R1 was disproportionately targeted by new manufacturing (associated with A2) in 2020.

Cluster R2 (isolated areas with some natural amenities experience little land use change) is associated with all Actors clusters to some degree, but mostly with A3 (slow growing population in urban areas) and A4 (slow growing population in rural areas). Though R2 counties have many natural amenities, their population growth remains low on the whole. This may be because of limited residential development opportunities, either limited by landscape or county policy.

An interesting combination is counties with R2-A1 (more urbanites) which persists in Blaine County. Blaine County historically attracted wealthy migrants looking to move to rural areas with amenities. Most places with A1 experience associated land use changes, but Blaine has not, which might make it an interesting case study.

Cluster R3 (isolated areas in dry shrublands experience little land use change) is associated primarily with clusters A3 and A4 (slow growing populations with low population density). Because of the US Census definition of urban, some of these counties may have transitioned from A4 to A3 over time as population centers reached the housing/population density threshold that defines urban. 

Cluster R4 (urban growth threatens farmland) is associated with A1 (more urbanites). This is a classic situation of farmland loss, where a growing urban population fuels development onto agricultural lands.

Cluster R5 (agricultural production areas with limited recreation and development) is associated mostly with A3 (slow growing population in urban areas). Because of the US Census definition of urban, some of these counties may have transitioned from A4 to A3 over time as population centers reached the housing/population density threshold that defines urban. 

## Cluster Transitions

No counties transitioned between resource clusters in the 40 years of this study, but that doesn't mean they don't change. For example, in cluster R4 (urban growth in the Treasure Valley), both counties are on trajectories towards more developed land and housing density. A similar shift occurs to a lesser degree in R1.

```{r}

  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,75)) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = bquote("Housing units per"~km^2)) +
  theme_classic()

p1+p2 + guide_area() +

              guides= "collect")

The dramatic increases in 2000 in Teton and Madison counties are accompanied by an actors transition to A1 (more urbanites)."
#| eval: false

Actors transitions are more common than Resource transitions.

Because of the US Census definition of urban, many counties may have transitioned from A4 to A3 over time because their population centers reached the housing/population density threshold that defines urban. 

Another common shift was from a number of Actors clusters (A1 and A3) to A2 (manufacturing provides additional rural employment) in 2020. This occurred mostly in R1, as well as in R2 and R5. Since this shift is so recent, it is difficult to assess the outcome of this shift, especially since it is impacting many different types of resource systems.

A transition that occurred in Elmore, Madison, and Teton counties in 2000 was a shift from A3 to A1. This indicates that population growth in their urban areas sped up, and the number of residents with Bachelors degrees increased. While Madison and Teton counties stayed in A1 for the remainder of the study period, Elmore County shifted back to A3 in 2010 and then to A2 in 2020. In Madison and Teton counties, the influx of new urban-area dwellers persisted, which seems to be followed by an increase in developed land and housing density that is unusual for their cluster (@fig-r1-shifts).

## NCP Outcomes of Archetypes

I only have NCP data for 2016-2020, so NCP must be analyzed as an outcome of the 40 years of archetypes. This section answers question 4.

```{r}
#| label: "get NCP data"
#| include: false
#| eval: false

# get list of file paths
NCP_data_files <- list.files("data/NCP_data", pattern = ".tif",
                             full.names = TRUE,
                             recursive = TRUE)

# read data files into list
NCP_data <- lapply(NCP_data_files, function(x) rast(x))
names(NCP_data) <- NCP_data_files %>%
  str_remove("../data/NCP_data/") %>%
  str_remove(".tif")

# check that all are aligned
# careful with this step - it may apply spatial functions that can warp data
template <- NCP_data[[1]]
aligned_rasts <- lapply(NCP_data, function(x) {
  if(crs(x) != crs(template)) {x <- project(x, template)}
  if(sum(res(x) != res(template)) > 0) {x <- resample(x, template)}
  if(sum(origin(x) != origin(template)) > 0) {x <- resample(x, template)}
  if(sum(ext(x) != ext(template)) > 0) {x <- resample(x, template)}
  
  return(x)
})

NCP_data <- rast(aligned_rasts)
names(NCP_data) <- names(aligned_rasts)
```

```{r}
#| label: "summarise NCP by county"
#| include: false
#| eval: false

max_min_NCP_layers <- as.numeric(lapply(NCP_data, FUN = function(x) {max(values(x), na.rm=T)})) - as.numeric(lapply(NCP_data, FUN = function(x) {min(values(x), na.rm=T)}))

NCP_sc <- scale(NCP_data,
                center = TRUE,
                scale = max_min_NCP_layers) #If scale is a numeric vector (recycled to nlyr(x)), each layer of x is divided by the corresponding value.

NCP_by_county_mean <- exact_extract(x = NCP_sc,
                               y = barcodes,
                               fun = "mean",
                               append_cols = c("county", "barcode"))
NCP_by_county_sd <- exact_extract(x = NCP_sc,
                               y = barcodes,
                               fun = "stdev",
                               append_cols = c("county", "barcode"))



# NCP_pca <- prcomp(NCP_sc[,-c(1:2)])
```

```{r}
#| label: "cluster NCP calcs"
#| include: false
#| eval: false

NCP_cats <- data.frame(NCP = names(NCP_data),
                       NCP_cat = c(rep("Climate Adaptation", 2),
                                   rep("C Stock Protection", 3),
                                   rep("Food and Feed", 4),
                                   rep("Habitat", 8),
                                   rep("Recreation", 2),
                                   rep("Water Quality", 2)))

NCP_means <- NCP_by_county_mean %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = !c("county", "barcode"),
               names_to = "NCP",
               values_to = "mean") %>%
  mutate(NCP = str_remove(NCP, "mean.")) %>%
  left_join(NCP_cats) %>%
  mutate(NCP = str_remove(NCP, regex("^data/NCP_data/[:print:]*/")))

NCP_stdev <- NCP_by_county_sd %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = !c("county", "barcode"),
               names_to = "NCP",
               values_to = "stdev") %>%
  mutate(NCP = str_remove(NCP, "stdev.")) %>%
  left_join(NCP_cats) %>%
  mutate(NCP = str_remove(NCP, regex("^data/NCP_data/[:print:]*/")))

NCP_means_sd <- left_join(NCP_means, NCP_stdev) %>%
  mutate(barcode.R = str_remove_all(barcode, regex("A[:digit:]{1}")),
         barcode.A = str_remove_all(barcode, regex("R[:digit:]{1}")))
```
```{r}
#| label: "fig-NCP-Rclusters"
#| fig-cap: "The range of mean 2016-2020 NCP values for each county in each Resource cluster pathway. Values are scaled so that 0 represents the mean of each NCP across the study area, so values below 0 are below average and above 0 are above average. I separated the 21 NCP layers I used in chapter 1 into the 6 NCP categories used in chapter 1, so even clusters with 2 counties (e.g. R5 = Ada and Canyon County) have >2 means in each category from multiple NCP layers."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| eval: false

ggplot(NCP_means_sd, aes(x=mean, y=barcode.R)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(vars(NCP_cat)) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    limits = rev(unique(NCP_means_sd$barcode.R)[order(unique(NCP_means_sd$barcode.R))]),
    labels = rev(c("R1", "R2", "R3", "R4", "R5"))) +
  labs(x = "Cluster mean (scaled values)", y = "Resource Cluster") +
  theme_bw()
```

_C Stock Protection:_ Cluster R2 provides above average C stock protection. This makes sense since R2 is associated with forested, mountainous areas.

_Climate Adaptation:_ Clusters R2 and R4 are areas with more ability to adapt to climate change. These are more likely to have A1 Actor clusters (more educated urbanites). This result points to issues of environmental justice, where more educated (so I'm assuming, more wealthy) actors are also the most well positioned to adapt to climate change. R1 also has A1 actors, but has other actor clusters as well, and this is reflected in the wide spread of climate adaptation NCP.

_Food and Feed:_ Resource clusters with potential for more croplands (R1, R4, R5) provide above average food and feed NCP.

_Habitat:_ The Resource clusters where agriculture and development are limited by rugged conditions (R3, and R2 to a lesser degree) generally provide higher than average habitat NCP. More agricultural (R5) and urban (R4) clusters generally provide less habitat on average, but they have a wide range, indicating that they provide different types of habitat NCP to different levels.

_Recreation:_ Most Resource clusters provide recreation NCP near the average for the study area.

_Water Quality:_ Most Resource clusters are near average here.

# Case Studies

In this section, I plan to expand on 2-4 counties in different clusters that present interesting cases, either because they are typical of their cluster or because they show unique characteristics. I'm thinking of Ada and/or Canyon (classic case of urban growth), Teton and/or Madison (non-urban farmland loss associated with A1 actors), and Blaine (a history of wealthy actors results in a "mimicry" of isolated areas). Available literature might influence this decision. For example, Haley has chapters on Owyhee, Blaine, and Teton counties in her dissertation.

# Main Takeaways

## Farmlands are threatened by more than urban growth

The original inspiration for this dissertation chapter was the observation that farmland loss prediction models underestimate farmland loss that isn't associated with urban growth. This analysis, and especially archetype R1, show that the average condition for this study area is farmland loss in places without large urban areas.

## Archetype analysis links spatially disparate but thematically similar counties

This analysis recontextualizes counties in the study area, allowing us to link counties that are spatially distant but have similar resources and actors. For example, though Twin Falls is far from Jefferson, both experience similar types of land use change and have the similar types of actors, and thus may borrow successful farmland protection strategies from each other. 

## Resource systems did not transition, even when actors changed. However, A1 actors in particular can lead to within-cluster shifts

Overall, I found that resource archetypes remained stable over this 40 year period while actor archetypes were more likely to change. This is reasonable for two reasons: (1) populations are more mobile than land systems, so it is easier for them to change, and (2) the difference between land systems (e.g. the dry shrublands of Owyhee and the forested recreation lands of Blaine) is greater than the difference between human populations, so it would require a greater change to shift resource archetypes compared to actor archetypes.

The presence of A1 actors (educated, growing, urban population) is associated with changes in resource systems, even if no counties transitioned from one resource archetype to another. Counties with A1 actors tend to accelerate their developed land growth and housing density. However, A1 does not always mean accelerated development, as evidenced by Blaine County, which has had wealthy inhabitants for a long time and has implemented land protections so that their resource system more closely matches more isolated counties.

## NCP -- ??

I need to think more about the NCP results and if they belong in this chapter. I don't find any surprising results here; the resource systems and their NCP outcomes all seem logical to me. Additionally, the NCP ranges seem to be either really wide or small and all centered on the average (recreation and water quality especially). Both those patterns are difficult to draw conclusions from.

-->

  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("land_in_farms", "percent_cropland", "percent_forest", "percent_shrubland", "perc_fed", "lake_area_km2", "rivers_km_per_km2", "percent_developed", "farms_per_acre", "perc_rec", "dist_to_ski", "dist_to_NP", "housing_units_per_acre", "perc_non_fed_road_area_km2", "healthworkers_per_1000", "perc_farms_change", "Perc_change_land_in_farms", "cropland_change", "forest_change", "shrub_change", "developed_change", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "ag_support_per_1000", "accom_food_per_1000", "med_home_val_in_2020_USD", "farm_size_pc1", "farm_size_pc2", "avg_slope"),
                                 labels = c("Land in Farms", "Cropland", "Forest", "Shrubland", "Federal Land", "Lake Area", "Length of Rivers", "Developed Land", "Farm Density", "Recreation Land", "Distance to a Ski Area", "Distance to a National Park", "Housing Density", "Non-Federal Land near Highway", "Healthcare Workers", "Farm Loss/Gain", "Land in Farms Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Developed Land Gain", "Farms with Net Loss", "Jobs Supporting Ag", "Jobs in Hospitality", "Med Home Value", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Farm Size (PC2)", "Average Slope"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get farm size raw data
# farm sizes range
# list parameters
params <- list(state_alpha = "ID",
               agg_level_desc = "county",
               year = c(2002, 2012, 2022),
               commodity_desc = "Farm operations",
               short_desc = "Farm operations - number of operations",
               domain_desc = "area operated")
# retrieve
farm_sizes <- nassqs(params)
# save a backup copy
# write.csv(farm_sizes,
#           "../data/API_data_download_backup/farm_sizes.csv",
#           row.names = FALSE)

# clean
farm_sizes2 <- farm_sizes %>%
  # remove redundant categories
  filter(!(domaincat_desc %in% c("AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 219 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (220 TO 259 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (260 TO 499 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (50.0 TO 69.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (70.0 TO 99.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (100 TO 139 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (140 TO 179 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (1,000 OR MORE ACRES)"))) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county_name, year),
              names_from = domaincat_desc,
              values_from = Value) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_farms = sum(c_across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`), na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`,
                ~.x/total_farms*100))

# 1992 data
farm_sizes_1992 <- read.csv("data/Farm_size_1925-1992.csv") %>%
  filter(Year == 1992) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("County", "Year"),
              names_from = "Size",
              values_from = "Num_farms") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(across(`under 10 acres`:`over 2,000 acres`,
                ~.x/`all farms`*100)) %>%
  # create comparable categories
  mutate(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)` = `1,000 to 1,999 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)` = `under 10 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)` = `10 to 49 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)` = `180 to 219 acres` + `220 to 259 acres` + `260 to 499 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)` = `over 2,000 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)` = `50 to 69 acres` + `70 to 99 acres` + `100 to 139 acres` + `140 to 179 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)` = `500 to 999 acres`) %>%
  rename("county_name" = "County",
         "year" = "Year")

# join
farm_sizes_all <- rbind(farm_sizes2[,1:9],
                        farm_sizes_1992[,c(1:2,16:22)]) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0) %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county_name),
         year = as.integer(year)-2)

farm_sizes_r1 <- left_join(r1, farm_sizes_all, by = c("county", "year")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(small_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)`),
         med_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)`),
         large_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`))
```

The counties in R1 are `r names(table(r1$county)[table(r1$county)==4])`, Bannock (1990-2000, 2020), Elmore (2020), and Power (1990).

### R3

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "R3 data"

r3 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]] %>%
  filter(cluster == "R3")

r3_means <- r3 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("land_in_farms", "percent_cropland", "percent_forest", "percent_shrubland", "perc_fed", "lake_area_km2", "rivers_km_per_km2", "percent_developed", "farms_per_acre", "perc_rec", "dist_to_ski", "dist_to_NP", "housing_units_per_acre", "perc_non_fed_road_area_km2", "healthworkers_per_1000", "perc_farms_change", "Perc_change_land_in_farms", "cropland_change", "forest_change", "shrub_change", "developed_change", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "ag_support_per_1000", "accom_food_per_1000", "med_home_val_in_2020_USD", "farm_size_pc1", "farm_size_pc2", "avg_slope"),
                                 labels = c("Land in Farms", "Cropland", "Forest", "Shrubland", "Federal Land", "Lake Area", "Length of Rivers", "Developed Land", "Farm Density", "Recreation Land", "Distance to a Ski Area", "Distance to a National Park", "Housing Density", "Non-Federal Land near Highway", "Healthcare Workers", "Farm Loss/Gain", "Land in Farms Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Developed Land Gain", "Farms with Net Loss", "Jobs Supporting Ag", "Jobs in Hospitality", "Med Home Value", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Farm Size (PC2)", "Average Slope"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

###############
# get farm size raw data
# farm sizes range
# list parameters
params <- list(state_alpha = "ID",
               agg_level_desc = "county",
               year = c(2002, 2012, 2022),
               commodity_desc = "Farm operations",
               short_desc = "Farm operations - number of operations",
               domain_desc = "area operated")
# retrieve
farm_sizes <- nassqs(params)
# save a backup copy
# write.csv(farm_sizes,
#           "../data/API_data_download_backup/farm_sizes.csv",
#           row.names = FALSE)

# clean
farm_sizes2 <- farm_sizes %>%
  # remove redundant categories
  filter(!(domaincat_desc %in% c("AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 219 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (220 TO 259 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (260 TO 499 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (50.0 TO 69.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (70.0 TO 99.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (100 TO 139 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (140 TO 179 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (1,000 OR MORE ACRES)"))) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county_name, year),
              names_from = domaincat_desc,
              values_from = Value) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_farms = sum(c_across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`), na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`,
                ~.x/total_farms*100))

# 1992 data
farm_sizes_1992 <- read.csv("data/Farm_size_1925-1992.csv") %>%
  filter(Year == 1992) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("County", "Year"),
              names_from = "Size",
              values_from = "Num_farms") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(across(`under 10 acres`:`over 2,000 acres`,
                ~.x/`all farms`*100)) %>%
  # create comparable categories
  mutate(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)` = `1,000 to 1,999 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)` = `under 10 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)` = `10 to 49 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)` = `180 to 219 acres` + `220 to 259 acres` + `260 to 499 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)` = `over 2,000 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)` = `50 to 69 acres` + `70 to 99 acres` + `100 to 139 acres` + `140 to 179 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)` = `500 to 999 acres`) %>%
  rename("county_name" = "County",
         "year" = "Year")

# join
farm_sizes_all <- rbind(farm_sizes2[,1:9],
                        farm_sizes_1992[,c(1:2,16:22)]) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0) %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county_name),
         year = as.integer(year)-2)

farm_sizes_r3 <- left_join(r3, farm_sizes_all, by = c("county", "year")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(small_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)`),
         med_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)`),
         large_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`))
```

The counties in R3 are `r names(table(r3$county)[table(r3$county)==4])`.

## Actors Archetypes


::: {#suppfigb-A-ranges}

```{r}
#| label: suppfigb-A-ranges
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 7.5

clust_dat_sc[["Actors"]] %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = !c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  left_join(ci_clust[["Actors"]][,c("cluster", "input_data_name", "sig")]) %>%
  mutate(sig = ifelse(is.na(sig), "Not in model", sig)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = input_data_name, fill = sig, alpha = sig, color=sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, color = "black", linetype="dashed") +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1,1)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(c("pop_per_acre", "perc_pop_change", "emply_pc1", "emply_pc2", "emply_pc3", "perc_retired", "avg_age", "med_income_in_2020_USD", "unemployment_rate", "High.school", "Bachelors", "races_PC1", "perc_hispanic", "tenure_pc1", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "num_hired", "pop_urban")),
                   labels = rev(c("Population Density", "Population Growth", "Employment Sectors (PC1)", "Employment Sectors (PC2)", "Employment Sectors (PC3)", "Percent Retired", "Average Age", "Median Household Income", "Unemployment Rate", "Residents with High School Education", "Residents with Bachelors", "Race (PC1)", "Percent Hispanic", "Full-Owned Farms", "Farms with Net Loss", "Hired Ag Workers", "Urban Population"))) +
  scale_fill_manual(limits = c("TRUE", "FALSE", "Not in model"),
                    values = c("orchid3", "orchid3", "beige"),
                    labels = c("Yes", "No", "Not in model\n(removed during\nvariable selection)"),
                    name = "Cluster mean\nsignificantly different\nfrom study area mean\n(p<0.05)") +
  scale_alpha_manual(limits = c("TRUE", "FALSE", "Not in model"),
                    values = c(1, 0.3, 0.3),
                    labels = c("Yes", "No", "Not in model\n(removed during\nvariable selection)"), 
                    name = "Cluster mean\nsignificantly different\nfrom study area mean\n(p<0.05)") +
  scale_color_manual(limits = c("TRUE", "FALSE", "Not in model"),
                    values = c("black", "gray50", "gray50"),
                    labels = c("Yes", "No", "Not in model\n(removed during\nvariable selection)"),
                    name = "Cluster mean\nsignificantly different\nfrom study area mean\n(p<0.05)") +
  facet_wrap(vars(cluster)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
